first.rationale: Two of the three current problems are internal funnel decay (activation -6%, onboarding completion -4%), and those are the levers most tied to sustainable qualified revenue rather than bought revenue. Two inherited memories converge on the same mechanism: memory_86 (shorter onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value) and memory_31 (signup simplification lifted SMB activation durably). Convergence across two independent records makes this the strongest-supported direction for the single slot. I deprioritize promotional_pricing despite memory_73's apparent fit with the competitor threat: matching aggressive entry pricing tends to buy price-sensitive, low-retention accounts, and memory_73 reports acquisition and revenue lift with no evidence of retained or qualified revenue, so it is the direction most likely to look good and score badly against the stated objective. Referral incentive (memory_57) treats established customers and does not touch the decaying funnel; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is a different segment from the one under attack and cannot move SMB activation this week. I spend the one verification pull on memory_86 rather than on a memory I am rejecting, because memory_86 is the load-bearing claim for the action I actually intend to take, and it is the one whose failure mode is invisible: 'completion rates up' can be a metric artifact of removing fields rather than real value delivery. I want the source record to show whether the lift persisted past week one and whether it held on revenue-relevant cohorts, not just completion counts. Key downstream risk I am carrying explicitly: reducing friction at signup and onboarding can admit lower-intent accounts, inflating activation while diluting qualified pipeline — the same trap as discounting, one step earlier in the funnel. So this runs as a controlled experiment with a holdout, and success is judged on downstream qualified revenue and retention at cohort maturity, not on completion or activation rate alone. If verification shows memory_86 measured only completion with no durability or quality follow-through, I downgrade to a small guarded test and treat the inherited claim as unproven rather than acting on it at standard scale. Both supporting memories are 24-52 days old and predate the competitor's entry pricing, so the SMB population they describe may no longer be the population I am acting on; I hold that as live uncertainty rather than resolving it in favor of the plan.

final.rationale: Verification strengthened the case rather than merely confirming the label. exp_86 reported not just completion +13% but two quality-side signals: time-to-value -2.1 days and 30-day retention +3%. That partially answers my main worry — that reduced friction would inflate top-of-funnel metrics while admitting lower-intent accounts — because retention moved in the same direction as completion rather than against it. A pure metric artifact would typically show completion up with retention flat or down. So I proceed at standard experiment scale rather than downgrading to a guarded test. This direction also has convergent support from memory_31 (signup simplification, durable SMB first-week activation lift), and it targets two of the three live problems directly: onboarding completion -4% and activation -6% are internal funnel decay, which is the kind of revenue that compounds rather than the kind that is bought. I continue to decline promotional_pricing despite its surface fit with the competitor's entry pricing. memory_73 reports acquisition and revenue lift with no retention or qualified-revenue evidence, and matching aggressive discounting recruits exactly the price-sensitive cohort most likely to churn — it would score well this quarter and badly against sustainable long-term qualified revenue. Referral incentive and enterprise_sales_assist address populations that are not the ones decaying this quarter and cannot move the observed funnel numbers in one week. Residual uncertainty I am carrying forward, not resolving: (1) exp_86's retention readout is at 30 days, which is shorter than the horizon that matters for qualified revenue — a +3% 30-day figure does not guarantee cohort-mature value; (2) both supporting memories predate the competitor's entry pricing by 24-52 days, so the SMB population I am acting on may have shifted composition toward more price-driven buyers than the one those experiments measured; (3) the two supporting memories describe adjacent but not identical interventions (signup fields vs. onboarding flow length), so their convergence is suggestive rather than a true replication. Execution accordingly: run with a holdout, and judge on downstream qualified revenue and retention at cohort maturity, with completion and activation treated as leading indicators only. If completion rises while qualified pipeline per cohort does not follow, I treat that as friction-removal admitting low-intent signups and roll back rather than scaling.
